papers.title_in_file: Efficient quantum algorithm for dissipative nonlinear differential equations
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v4 (7 Jul 2026); record year 2026 matches. Same title as record.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sec. 1 (Introduction), statements of Theorems 1 and 2, Sec. 5 (lower bound) opening, Sec. 6 (applications) epidemiology example. Proofs in Sec. 3 and 4 not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: A quantum algorithm paper: Carleman linearization plus forward Euler plus the quantum linear system algorithm for dissipative quadratic ODEs, with a complexity upper bound for R < 1 and a lower bound for strongly nonlinear cases.

assertions.value: For dissipative quadratic n-dimensional ODEs, assuming R < 1 (R characterizes the ratio of the nonlinearity and forcing to the linear dissipation), the paper gives a quantum algorithm whose complexity has polylogarithmic dependence on T, n and 1/error, and which it describes as an exponential improvement over previous quantum algorithms, whose complexity is exponential in T.
quotes: This is an exponential improvement over the best previous quantum algorithms, whose complexity is exponential in
Assuming R < 1, where R is a parameter characterizing the ratio of the nonlinearity and forcing to the linear dissipation
assertions.certainty_reason: Analytic complexity bound with proof (Theorem 1) under stated assumptions; the comparison is to earlier quantum algorithms, not classical ones.

assertions.value: The paper states that the algorithm is efficient only if the solution does not decay exponentially in T (the dependence on q); for homogeneous ODEs with R < 1 the solution necessarily decays exponentially, so the algorithm is not asymptotically efficient there, while driven (inhomogeneous) equations can avoid this.
quotes: Note that the solution cannot decay exponentially in T for the algorithm to be efficient, as captured by the dependence of the complexity on q
For homogeneous ODEs with R < 1, the solution necessarily decays exponentially in time (see equation (4.11)), so the algorithm is not asymptotically efficient.
While exponential decay precludes efficiency, driven equations can avoid this issue despite the presence of dissipation.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' analytic statement about the scope of their own bound.

assertions.value: The paper gives a lower bound on worst-case quantum complexity for general quadratic differential equations, showing the problem is intractable for R at least 2; the range 1 <= R < 2 is stated as open.
quotes: We also provide a lower bound on the worst-case complexity of quantum algorithms for general quadratic differential equations, showing that the problem is intractable for
Whereas there is an efficient quantum algorithm for R < 1 (as shown in Theorem 1), we show here that the problem is intractable for
assertions.certainty_reason: Proved information-theoretic argument (distinguishing nonorthogonal states) in Theorem 2.
assertions.reader_inference: The threshold R >= 2 is read from a glyph that lost its symbol in text extraction; the open range for 1 <= R < 2 is stated in the paper.

assertions.value: The paper states that the R < 1 condition can be satisfied in realistic epidemiological models; for one stated parameter set it computes R = 0.956.
quotes: showing that the R < 1 condition can be satisfied in realistic epidemiological models and giving numerical evidence that the method may describe a model of fluid dynamics even for larger values of R
With the stated parameters, a direct calculation gives R = 0.956 and ensures
assertions.certainty_reason: Calculation for one chosen parameter set of a compartment model; the fluid-dynamics statement is numerical evidence only.

papers.title_in_file: CutQC: Using Small Quantum Computers for Large Quantum Circuit Evaluations
papers.version_note: Printed as the ASPLOS '21 version; matches record.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sec. 1, Sec. 2 background, start of Sec. 4, Sec. 5 benchmarks setup, Sec. 6 evaluation (FD/DD query, runtime, real-device fidelity), related-work comparison. Cut-search MIP formulas not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: A systems paper: a hybrid method that cuts a large quantum circuit into subcircuits run on smaller devices and reconstructs the output classically, evaluated by simulation and on IBM devices.

assertions.value: The paper introduces CutQC, which cuts large quantum circuits into smaller subcircuits executed on smaller quantum devices, with classical postprocessing reconstructing the output of the original circuit.
quotes: CutQC cuts large quantum circuits into smaller subcircuits, allowing them to be executed on smaller quantum devices. Classical postprocessing can then reconstruct the output of the original circuit.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' description of their own method, backed by their experiments.

assertions.value: In full-state (FD) query tests on 10-, 15-, 20- and 25-qubit quantum computers using 16 compute nodes for postprocessing, the paper reports an average of 60X to 8600X runtime speedup over classical simulation across its benchmarks; the subcircuits were executed with statevector simulation, not on hardware.
quotes: We achieve an average of 60X to 8600X runtime speedup over classical simulation for our benchmarks.

Because NISQ devices currently do not allow high-fidelity executions of circuits beyond just a few qubits, we executed the subcircuits with statevector simulation to demonstrate the effectiveness of our postprocessing techniques.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured postprocessing runtime on one cluster setup; the quantum part is simulated, so the speedup is of the hybrid postprocessing against full-state classical simulation.
assertions.reader_inference: The speedup baseline is full-state classical simulation; the paper itself notes other classical simulation techniques are hard to compare directly.

assertions.value: On IBM hardware, the paper compares CutQC on the 5-qubit Bogota device with direct execution on the 20-qubit Johannesburg device and reports an average 21% to 47% improvement to chi-square loss across benchmarks; it states that direct execution beyond 12 qubits fails to produce meaningful output.
quotes: We show an average of 21% to 47% improvement to
for different benchmarks by using CutQC with small quantum computers, as compared with direct executions on large quantum computers.
The experiments stop at 12 qubits because QC evaluation beyond this point succumbs to the effects of noise and fails to produce meaningful output.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured on two specific IBM devices at 2020-era noise levels, circuits of up to 12 qubits.

assertions.value: The paper tested DD query on circuits of up to 100 qubits, but because no backend could produce accurate executions at that scale it used uniform distributions as the subcircuit output, so that test studies runtime only.
quotes: We tested DD query for circuits up to 100 qubits, significantly beyond the current classical and quantum limit.
Because no backends are capable of producing accurate circuit executions on this scale, we used uniform distributions as the subcircuit output to study the runtime.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors state the limitation of their own experiment.

papers.version_note: File is arXiv v2 (14 Oct 2025), titled Beyond-classical computation in quantum simulation; the file name carries the v1 title Computational supremacy in quantum simulation. Matches the record title.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Classical simulation techniques, results on 2D lattices (Figs. 2-3), higher-dimensional topologies (Fig. 4), Fig. 5 and resource estimate, Summary. Supplementary Material in the file not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: An experimental paper by D-Wave authors: superconducting quantum annealers simulate quench dynamics of transverse-field Ising spin glasses, compared with MPS, PEPS and neural-quantum-state classical methods.

assertions.value: The authors state that superconducting quantum annealing processors rapidly generate samples in close agreement with Schroedinger-equation solutions for quench dynamics of spin glasses, and that several leading approximate tensor-network and neural-network methods cannot reach the same accuracy within a reasonable time frame.
quotes: Here we show that superconducting quantum annealing processors can rapidly generate samples in close agreement with solutions of the
We show that several leading approximate methods based on tensor networks and neural networks cannot achieve the same accuracy as the quantum annealer within a reasonable time frame.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors, employed by the QPU vendor, report measurements and classical comparisons; the large-scale part is extrapolated.

assertions.value: By extrapolating the MPS cost needed to match QPU quality, the authors state that on the largest problems MPS would take millions of years on the Frontier supercomputer per input; they state this applies to MPS only and is not an intrinsic lower bound for all classical methods.
quotes: On the largest problems, MPS would take millions of years on the Frontier supercomputer per input to match QPU quality.

We emphasize that this scaling analysis applies to MPS--the only method with which we can match QPU quality for all considered quench times--and is not an intrinsic lower bound for all classical methods.
assertions.certainty_reason: Extrapolation from simulable sizes under assumed perfect parallelization; authors explicitly say it is not a lower bound for all classical methods.

assertions.value: The authors report that PEPS and NQS methods struggle for slower quenches (annealing time 20 ns) even on relatively small systems, and that ground-truth verification can only be done at small scales where it can be computed.
assertions.anchor: Sec. on classical methods, p. 4; Intro p. 2
quotes: In contrast, we found that PEPS and NQS methods struggle for slower quenches (ta=20 ns), even for those relatively small systems.
This direct, nonuniversal verification can only be achieved at small scales, where the ground truth can be computed.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured by the authors on 2D lattices up to 8x8 against their own MPS ground truth.

assertions.value: On the largest lattice of each topology for which the MPS ground truth is converged, at annealing times 7 ns and 20 ns, the authors report a median deviation of only 1% between quantum and classical simulation in the spin-glass order parameter.
quotes: The resulting quantities have a median deviation of only 1% between quantum and classical simulation.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured on 20-instance ensembles at simulable sizes only.

papers.title_in_file: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Generative Adversarial Network for High Resolution Image Generation
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v2 (20 Jan 2023); matches record.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Sec. IV framework overview, Sec. V setup, Sec. VI results, Sec. VII parameter study, Sec. VIII conclusions. Related work and appendices skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A QML paper proposing PQWGAN, a patch quantum generator trained with the WGAN-GP objective and a classical critic, evaluated by noiseless simulation on MNIST and Fashion MNIST subsets.

assertions.value: The authors claim that, to the best of their knowledge, theirs is the first QGAN with a quantum generator that successfully generates 28x28 images without dimensionality reduction or classical pre/post-processing at this scale.
quotes: this is the first demonstration of a QGAN that uses quantum circuits as a generator that can successfully generate images without dimensionality reduction or classical pre/post-processing at this scale.
assertions.certainty_reason: Priority claim by the authors, hedged by to the best of our knowledge.

assertions.value: In noiseless simulation, the authors report PQWGAN generated images comparable to a classical WGAN-GP with 3 orders of magnitude fewer generator parameters (5376 quantum against roughly 1.46 million classical); a classical generator with similar parameter count could not learn anything meaningful.
quotes: For our WGAN-GP architecture, the generator consists of roughly 1.46 million trainable parameters while our quantum generator consists of 5376 trainable parameters.
In comparison, a classical generator with a similar parameter count is unable to learn anything meaningful.
our PQWGAN was able to achieve comparable results despite having 3 orders of magnitude less trainable parameters in the generator.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-setup simulations on 2 to 3 classes with visual comparison; no quantitative image-quality metric was seen in the passages read.
assertions.reader_inference: Training used only the first 1000 samples per class and 600 generator iterations, and the comparison appears to rest on visual inspection of samples.

assertions.value: All PQWGAN training was simulated without noise, and training used only the first 1000 samples of every included class; the authors list noise models and physical devices as future work.
quotes: The training of all PQWGANs are simulated without noise using high performance computing resources from the National Computational Infrastructure, Pawsey and the University of Melbourne.
Due to resource limitations, we will only be using the first 1000 samples of every class that we include in our training set
First, our work here is based solely on noiseless simulations.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' statement of their experimental conditions.

assertions.value: For MNIST digits 0/1/3, both PQWGAN and WGAN-GP start to struggle, and PQWGAN outputs show artifacts at the same location in every image whose cause is not fully known; with only 1 patch the generator fails to output anything meaningful.
quotes: However, for MNIST 0/1/3 both the PQWGAN and WGAN-GP starts to struggle.
However, for the PQWGAN, there are now artifacts that persist in the same location of every output image. The reason for such simulation results is not fully known.
Starting with only 1 patch, the generator fails to output anything meaningful.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors report their own negative observations from simulations.

papers.version_note: File is arXiv v1 (June 2020); matches record.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sec. 1 introduction, quantum-neuron overview, Sec. 4 experiments (4.1-4.5 incl. Table 1 and DNA task), Sec. 5 conclusion. Mathematical derivation of cell and gradient analysis skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A QML paper constructing a quantum recurrent neural network cell from parametrized quantum neurons with amplitude amplification, implemented in pytorch and tested on sequence and MNIST tasks by simulation.

assertions.value: The author states he constructs a quantum recurrent neural network built from parametrized quantum neurons with amplitude amplification, with demonstrable performance on sequence learning and integer digit classification.
quotes: In this work we construct a quantum recurrent neural network (QRNN) with demonstrable performance on non-trivial tasks such as sequence learning and integer digit classification.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author's summary of results obtained in classical simulation.

assertions.value: The author states that existing recurrent models, even simple RNNs, outclass the proposed QRNN on real-world learning tasks, in part because simulating many qubits classically needs memory that grows exponentially in the workspace size, which limits the number of parameters.
quotes: Without doubt, existing recurrent models--even simple RNNs--outclass the proposed QRNN architecture in this paper in real-world learning tasks.
In part, this is because we cannot easily simulate a large number of qubits on classical hardware: the memory requirements necessarily grow exponentially in the size of the workspace
assertions.certainty_reason: Explicit limitation stated by the author in the conclusion.

assertions.value: On a DNA sequence recognition task, a QRNN with 837 parameters trained in an almost constant number of steps up to string lengths of 1000 bases, while an LSTM with 888 parameters began faster but ended with more than order-of-magnitude worse performance in this test; RNN and LSTM baselines used stock pytorch settings besides learning rate.
quotes: We found that a QRNN with a workspace size of 5, one work stage, and activation degree 3 (resulting in 837 parameters) can be trained within an almost constant number of steps, even for string lengths of 1000 bases.
the LSTM shows a steady increase--starting out faster than the QRNN, but ending up with a more than order-of-magnitude worse performance in this test.
assertions.certainty_reason: One synthetic task, simulation only, baselines tuned only for learning rate; the author's footnote says baselines could improve with more tuning.

assertions.value: For MNIST, images were cropped to 20x20, downscaled to 10x10 and binarized, giving an input sequence of length 100; the author states this significantly reduces the information content and that the model is not competing with top-of-the-line classifiers.
quotes: Naturally, this significantly reduces the information content of the training data; yet as we are not competing with top-of-the-line classifiers with our QRNN model
assertions.certainty_reason: Author's statement of the experimental preprocessing and its purpose.

papers.title_in_file: Fermionic quantum processing with programmable neutral atom arrays
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v1 (13 Mar 2023); matches record.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Sec. I introduction, Sec. II-III gate decompositions, VQE example, Sec. V experimental challenges, Sec. VI conclusions. Appendix derivations skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A theory and proposal paper for a fermionic quantum processor on tweezer arrays of fermionic atoms, with gate protocols and circuit decompositions for quantum chemistry and lattice gauge theory; no experiment reported in the passages read.

assertions.value: The paper proposes a fermionic quantum processor in which fermionic models are locally encoded in a fermionic register using fermionic atoms in tweezer arrays, and states the encoding overhead of qubit-based devices as the motivation.
quotes: we present a fermionic quantum processor, where fermionic models are locally encoded in a fermionic register and simulated in a

Although qubit-based quantum computers can potentially tackle this problem more efficiently than classical devices, encoding non-local fermionic statistics introduces an overhead in the required resources
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' proposal and framing; not an experimental result.

assertions.value: The paper states that its decompositions of the pair-tunneling and density-dependent tunneling gates in the fermionic gate set have constant circuit depth of 5 gates, exact and optimal, which it says is a clear depth advantage over Jordan-Wigner circuits.
quotes: Both decompositions have a constant circuit depth of 5 gates and are exact and optimal.
This provides a clear advantage in terms of depth with respect to the circuit obtained using e.g. JW transformations
assertions.certainty_reason: Analytic circuit decomposition by the authors; hardware-dependent assumptions (all-to-all connectivity of atom arrays).

assertions.value: The authors discuss experimental challenges that must be overcome to build the processor, and state that a detailed study for larger molecules with ADAPT-VQE is deferred to a separate work, where the advantage of fermionic processing is expected to grow with the number of orbitals.
quotes: We finish by discussing in more detail some of the experimental challenges that should be overcome to build a fermionic quantum processor
where the advantage of fermionic processing compared to qubitbased protocols is expected to grow with the number of orbitals
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' expectation and acknowledgment of open hardware challenges, not a measurement.
assertions.reader_inference: No hardware demonstration of the processor was seen in the sections read.

papers.title_in_file: Experimental quantum computational chemistry with optimised unitary coupled cluster ansatz
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v3 (17 Jun 2024); title matches record. The file name carries the earlier v1 title Scalable quantum computational chemistry with superconducting qubits.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, main text through conclusion, Fig. 1-4 captions. Supplementary sections in the file not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: An experimental paper: VQE with an optimised UCC ansatz and error mitigation on the 66-qubit Zuchongzhi 2.0 superconducting processor, using up to 12 qubits for H2, LiH and F2.

assertions.value: The authors report scaling VQE with an optimised UCC ansatz to 12 qubits on a superconducting processor and achieving chemical accuracy for H2 at all bond distances and LiH at small bond distances.
quotes: we push forward the limit of experimental quantum computational chemistry and successfully scale up the implementation of VQE with an optimised unitary coupled-cluster ansatz to 12 qubits.
We achieve chemical accuracy for H2 at all bond distances and LiH at small bond distances in the experiment
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured on one device with error mitigation; H2 uses 4 qubits and LiH 6 qubits, the 12-qubit run is F2.

assertions.value: For F2 (12 qubits) the energy errors are around 10-2 to 10-1, above the chemical accuracy threshold; the raw errors for LiH and F2 are above 0.1 Hartree and 1 Hartree respectively, and accuracy is lower for larger systems.
quotes: Owing to the larger system size and deeper circuit, the energy errors for F2 are around 10-2 to 10-1, above the chemical accuracy threshold.
The raw experiment results indicate that the simulation becomes less accurate with increasing system size.
For instance, the raw errors for LiH and F2 are above 0.1 Hartree and 1 Hartree, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured negative result reported by the authors for the largest molecule.

assertions.value: On the 66-qubit Zuchongzhi 2.0 processor with 12 selected qubits, combining readout error mitigation, Clifford fitting, symmetry verification and CMX, the authors report energy-error suppression of around two orders of magnitude for H2, LiH and F2.
quotes: We demonstrate a significant enhancement of the accuracy by around two orders of magnitude with error mitigation techniques.
The experiment is conducted on a 66-qubit superconducting quantum processor
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured comparison of raw and mitigated energies on one device.

assertions.value: The authors state the current processor is insufficient for larger molecules because of hardware errors, and that readout errors dominate for small molecules while gate errors become more serious as system size increases.
quotes: While owing to non-negligible hardware errors, the current quantum processor is insufficient for larger molecules, the variational scheme is tested to be effective and reliable in our experimental implementation.
Our findings indicate that readout errors dominate for small molecules, while gate errors become more serious when the system size increases.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own error analysis (Fig. 4c) and stated limitation.
